docs.title: D01 · Python intro, arithmetic and variables
docs.text:
Unit: DS 1.1 Python Fundamentals · Day 1 of 14

What to do today

Read this brief, then download and run the lesson notebook from Downloads.

Concept taught

What a program is and how Python runs one: the interpreter reads a cell top to bottom, print() is how a value becomes visible, and a comment is text for the human reader that the interpreter skips. The lesson also sets the working habit of the whole course: run a cell, read the output, compare it with what you expected.

By the end of this lesson you can

  1. Run a cell in Jupyter and locate its output and its error text.
  2. Use print() to display a literal, a calculation and several values in one call.
  3. Write a comment that says why a line exists, not what it does.
  4. Describe in one sentence what the interpreter does with a line of code.

Why this matters

Every notebook in the credential is a program, and every assessment is marked on code plus a written justification, so the comment habit starts here. Reading an error message calmly is the single skill that most separates students who finish a code-along from those who stall.

docs.title: D01 · Python intro, arithmetic and variables
docs.text:
Unit: DS 1.1 Python Fundamentals · Day 1 of 14

What to do today

Read this brief, then download and run the lesson notebook from Downloads.

Concept taught

Python as a calculator, then as a memory. The seven arithmetic operators including floor division, modulo and power; precedence; the difference between an int and a float and when division makes one from the other; variables as named storage that can be reassigned; naming rules; and conversion between int, float and str.

By the end of this lesson you can

  1. Evaluate an expression with mixed operators using the correct precedence.
  2. Predict whether a result is an int or a float before running the cell.
  3. Store a value in a well-named variable and reuse it in a later expression.
  4. Convert between int, float and str, and explain when a conversion fails.

Why this matters

Unit conversions, cost calculations and every formula later in the course (standard error on DS 1.2 D14, RMSE on D20) are arithmetic on variables. The int versus float distinction returns as the NumPy dtype on D09, where it decides whether a column can hold a decimal at all.

docs.title: D02 · Strings and formatting
docs.text:
Unit: DS 1.1 Python Fundamentals · Day 2 of 14

What to do today

Read this brief, then download and run the lesson notebook from Downloads.

Concept taught

Text as a sequence: creating strings with either quote, concatenation and repetition, indexing single characters (including negative positions), slicing ranges with start:stop:step, the common methods (upper, lower, strip, split, replace, find, count), and f-strings for formatted output with width and precision. Strings are immutable, so every method returns a new string.

By the end of this lesson you can

  1. Index and slice a string to extract a character or a substring, including from the end.
  2. Apply string methods to clean and reshape text, and explain why the original is unchanged.
  3. Format a sentence with an f-string, controlling decimal places and column width.
  4. Split a delimited line into parts and join them back with a different separator.

Why this matters

Raw data is text: names, codes, addresses, dates as strings. The methods here become the pandas .str accessor on D13 and the regex work of DS 1.2 D08. Slicing syntax is reused unchanged on lists (D06) and arrays (D09).

docs.title: D03 · Logic and conditionals
docs.text:
Unit: DS 1.1 Python Fundamentals · Day 3 of 14

What to do today

Read this brief, then download and run the lesson notebook from Downloads.

Concept taught

Decisions in code. Booleans as values, the six comparison operators, combining conditions with and, or and not, and if/elif/else with correct ordering and nesting. The emphasis is on predicting the value of a condition before the branch runs.

By the end of this lesson you can

  1. Predict the result of a comparison, including between a number and a string.
  2. Combine conditions with and, or and not, and explain the order of evaluation.
  3. Write an if/elif/else chain whose branches are ordered so every case is reachable.
  4. Trace a nested conditional by hand and state which branch runs for a given input.

Why this matters

A boolean mask on D09 and a pandas filter on D12 are exactly these comparisons applied to a whole column at once. Every business rule ('flag orders above the threshold', 'treat the missing value as zero') is a conditional.

docs.title: D04 · Loops and iteration
docs.text:
Unit: DS 1.1 Python Fundamentals · Day 4 of 14

What to do today

Read this brief, then download and run the lesson notebook from Downloads.

Concept taught

Repetition. The while loop for 'until a condition changes', the for loop for 'over each item', range with start, stop and step, break and continue, and the accumulator pattern (a running total or count updated inside the loop). Infinite loops and off-by-one errors are demonstrated, not just warned about.

By the end of this lesson you can

  1. Choose between while and for from the shape of the problem.
  2. Iterate over a range with a step and predict the last value printed.
  3. Accumulate a total, a count or a maximum inside a loop.
  4. Stop a loop early with break and explain when continue is the better tool.

Why this matters

Loops are how every row and every file is processed before pandas exists, and the Password System case study is one loop around one conditional. Knowing the loop is what makes vectorisation on D09 meaningful: it is the loop you no longer write.

docs.text:
Unit: DS 1.1 Python Fundamentals · Day 5 of 14

What to do today

Read this brief, then download and run the lesson notebook from Downloads.

Concept taught

Reusable code with a name. Defining a function with parameters, calling it, returning a value versus printing one, default arguments, a docstring, and the DRY principle as the reason to write one. Variables created inside a function are shown to be local.

By the end of this lesson you can

  1. Define a function with parameters and a return value and call it with different inputs.
  2. Distinguish a function that returns from one that prints, and say which a caller can reuse.
  3. Give a parameter a default and call the function with and without it.
  4. Refactor two repeated blocks into one function without changing the output.

Why this matters

apply() on D13 takes a function; every reusable analysis step in DS 1.2 and DS 1.3 is one. Assessments from here on mark a task down when a value is printed instead of returned, because a printed value cannot be tested.

docs.title: D06 · Lists and tuples
docs.text:
Unit: DS 1.1 Python Fundamentals · Day 6 of 14

What to do today

Read this brief, then download and run the lesson notebook from Downloads.

Concept taught

Ordered collections. Lists that can change (append, extend, insert, remove, pop, sort), slicing reused from strings, looping over a list, enumerate for the index and the item together, tuples as the immutable form, lambda as a throwaway function for a sort key, and the list comprehension as a whole-collection transform in one expression.

By the end of this lesson you can

  1. Build, extend and reorder a list, and predict its contents after each method call.
  2. Slice a list and explain why the result is a new list.
  3. Loop with enumerate to use both the position and the value.
  4. Choose a tuple over a list and state what the choice guarantees.
  5. Rewrite a for-loop that builds a list as a comprehension, and sort with a lambda key.

Why this matters

A DataFrame column behaves like a list; a NumPy shape is a tuple; groupby keys come back as tuples. The comprehension is the bridge to vectorised thinking, and the lambda returns inside sort, apply and key arguments across the whole credential.

docs.title: D07 · Dictionaries and sets
docs.text:
Unit: DS 1.1 Python Fundamentals · Day 7 of 14

What to do today

Read this brief, then download and run the lesson notebook from Downloads.

Concept taught

Lookup by key. Creating and reading dictionaries, adding and changing entries, the methods (keys, values, items, get, update), iterating over pairs, nested dictionaries, and counting with a dictionary. Sets for uniqueness and membership, with union, intersection and difference.

By the end of this lesson you can

  1. Look up, add and update a value by key, and use get() so a missing key does not crash.
  2. Iterate over a dictionary's items and build a second dictionary from the first.
  3. Count occurrences of items with a dictionary.
  4. Deduplicate a list with a set and test membership in constant time.
  5. Choose between a list and a dictionary from how the data will be looked up.

Why this matters

JSON on D08 is dictionaries and lists all the way down. A DataFrame is built from a dictionary of columns on D11, and recoding a column (map a code to a label) is a dictionary lookup. Sets are how you check which IDs are in one table but not another.

docs.title: D08 · Reading data files: CSV, Excel, PDF
docs.text:
Unit: DS 1.1 Python Fundamentals · Day 8 of 14

What to do today

Read this brief, then download and run the lesson notebook from Downloads.

Concept taught

Getting data in and out of a program. Opening files with a with-block, the modes, reading whole files and line by line, writing, parsing a delimited line into fields, the difference between bytes and text, JSON load and dump, and CSV through the csv module. Paths are handled explicitly so a missing file is a readable error.

By the end of this lesson you can

  1. Read and write a text file inside a with-block and explain why the block closes the file.
  2. Parse delimited lines into lists and dictionaries, converting fields to numbers.
  3. Load a JSON file into nested dictionaries and lists, and write one back.
  4. Read a CSV with csv.DictReader and compute a total from one column.
  5. Handle a missing file with a clear message instead of a traceback.

Why this matters

pd.read_csv on D11 does all of this in one call; knowing what is underneath is what explains encoding, delimiter and quoting errors when it fails. Every project in the credential begins by loading a file, and the spine dataset enters here.

Unit: DS 1.1 Python Fundamentals · Day 8 of 14

What to do today

Read this brief, then download and run the lesson notebook from Downloads.

Concept taught

Text that is locked inside a PDF. Installing pypdf, opening a document, extracting text page by page, splitting it into lines, saving the result to a text file, and recognising the common failure: a scanned PDF with no text layer, which needs OCR rather than parsing.

By the end of this lesson you can

  1. Extract the text of every page of a PDF into a single string.
  2. Split extracted text into lines and pull out the lines that match a target.
  3. Save extracted text to a file for later processing.
  4. Recognise from empty output that a PDF is an image and say what would be needed instead.

Why this matters

Reports, invoices, annual accounts and government statistics arrive as PDFs. The extracted text feeds regex cleaning on DS 1.2 D08 and the NLP pipeline on D11.

docs.title: D09 · NumPy arrays, aggregation and masking
docs.text:
Unit: DS 1.1 Python Fundamentals · Day 9 of 14

What to do today

Read this brief, then download and run the lesson notebook from Downloads.

Concept taught

The array. Creating arrays from lists and with generators (zeros, ones, arange, linspace), shape and dtype, arithmetic on whole arrays without a loop, aggregation (sum, mean, min, max, std) along an axis, indexing and slicing in one and two dimensions, and the boolean mask: a comparison applied to the whole array used to select elements.

By the end of this lesson you can

  1. Create an array of a given shape and dtype and read both back.
  2. Replace a D04 loop with a single vectorised expression and show the results match.
  3. Aggregate a 2-D array along rows and along columns and say which axis is which.
  4. Select elements with a boolean mask built from a comparison.
  5. Explain why an int array cannot hold a decimal and what happens when you try.

Why this matters

pandas sits on NumPy, so every column operation on D11 onward is an array operation. Every statistic in DS 1.2 D13 is an aggregation; every filter is a mask; images and model weights in DS 1.3 are arrays.

docs.text:
Unit: DS 1.1 Python Fundamentals · Day 10 of 14

What to do today

Read this brief, then download and run the lesson notebook from Downloads.

Concept taught

Arrays of different shapes working together. The broadcasting rules and how to predict whether two shapes are compatible, fancy indexing with an array of positions, argsort for sorting one array by another, stacking and splitting, and matrix operations (dot product, transpose). Centering data by subtracting a column mean is the worked example.

By the end of this lesson you can

  1. Predict whether two shapes broadcast and what the result shape is.
  2. Standardise every column of a 2-D array in one expression.
  3. Select rows with an index array and reorder an array with argsort.
  4. Stack arrays vertically and horizontally and predict the shape.
  5. Compute a dot product and check it against the loop version.

Why this matters

Standardising features is broadcasting; 'top ten' is argsort; the dot product is how regression on DS 1.2 D19 and every neural-network layer in DS 1.3 computes. A student who can predict a broadcast shape can read a shape-mismatch error.

docs.text:
Unit: DS 1.1 Python Fundamentals · Day 12 of 14

What to do today

Read this brief, then download and run the lesson notebook from Downloads.

Concept taught

Reshaping a table to answer a question. Selecting with loc and iloc, filtering with boolean conditions combined with & and |, sorting by one or several keys, finding and handling missing values (isna, dropna, fillna), groupby with aggregation, and merging two tables with a check on the row count afterwards.

By the end of this lesson you can

  1. Select rows and columns with loc and iloc and say when each is the right tool.
  2. Filter with two conditions combined and predict the number of rows returned.
  3. Sort by two keys in different directions.
  4. Count missing values per column and choose between dropping and filling.
  5. Group by a category and compute several aggregates in one call.
  6. Merge two tables and explain any change in row count.

Why this matters

Most of an analyst's day is this lesson. The Chipotle assessment is entirely filtering, grouping and a per-order rate; DS 1.2 D04 to D07 assume all of it is fluent, and the merge row-count check is the habit that catches duplicated keys.

What to do today

Read this brief, then download and run the lesson notebook from Downloads.

Concept taught

Making new columns. apply with a function from D05 on a column and on a row, np.where for a conditional column, converting text to datetime and extracting year, month and weekday, the .str accessor for text columns, and pivot tables as a two-way groupby.

By the end of this lesson you can

  1. Apply a named function and a lambda to a column and produce a new column.
  2. Create a conditional column with np.where instead of a loop.
  3. Convert a string column to datetime and extract month and day of week.
  4. Build a pivot table and read it back as a groupby with two keys.

Why this matters

This is feature engineering by another name. Month and weekday columns drive most business charts; apply and np.where are how DS 1.2 recodes categories and DS 1.3 builds features.

Unit: DS 1.1 Python Fundamentals · Day 13 of 14

What to do today

Read this brief, then download and run the lesson notebook from Downloads.

Concept taught

Time as an index. Timestamps and DatetimeIndex, to_datetime with formats, date ranges, slicing by date, resampling to a coarser frequency with the right aggregation (size for counts, sum for totals, mean for rates), rolling windows and shifting for change over time.

By the end of this lesson you can

  1. Parse dates with to_datetime, including a non-default format, and set them as the index.
  2. Slice a time-indexed frame by a date range.
  3. Resample daily data to weekly or monthly and choose the aggregation that answers the question.
  4. Compute a rolling mean and explain what the window does to noise.
  5. State what resample('D').size() counts and why it differs from sum().

Why this matters

Sales by month, daily rides, sensor readings and website traffic are all this. The taxi resample built here is the exact first step of the ARIMA paper on DS 1.2 D21.

Unit: DS 1.1 Python Fundamentals · Day 14 of 14

What to do today

Read this brief, then download and run the lesson notebook from Downloads.

Concept taught

The same questions asked of a database. Connecting to SQLite, SELECT with WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY and JOIN, pulling results into a DataFrame with read_sql, and the pandas equivalent of each query side by side. Inner versus left join semantics are shown with row counts, which is also the explanation of merge on D12.

By the end of this lesson you can

  1. Query a database table into a DataFrame.
  2. Write a SELECT with a filter, a group and an ordering, and reproduce it in pandas.
  3. Join two tables and predict the row count for inner and left joins.
  4. Decide which part of an analysis to run in SQL and which in pandas, and say why.

Why this matters

Enterprise data lives in databases, and filtering at the database before loading is the difference between a query that runs and one that exhausts memory. Join semantics learned here explain every surprising merge for the rest of the credential.
